source.title: Scale or Reason? A Compute-Equivalent Analysis of Reasoning Distillation
source.authors: Nicolas Boizard; Hippolyte Gisserot-Boukhlef; Kevin El Haddad; C. Hudelot; Pierre Colombo

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no material truncation or garbling noted.
record.tranche_reason: It tests downstream accuracy as model size and training or inference FLOPs vary, using post-training students rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. as background, but does not test their held-out pretraining-loss laws or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its own downstream accuracy sweeps and saturating fits bear on V6. The fitted curves are described as saturating growth functions, not power laws.
record.test_reason: Downstream accuracy is reported for five Qwen2.5 student sizes (0.5B–14B) after IFT or reasoning distillation, which bears on V6 in a post-training setting. The study's main question is format efficiency at matched FLOPs, not scaling laws. No pretraining loss, token/parameter allocation or architecture shape is studied, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors conclude that at matched training and inference FLOPs, IFT lies on or near the Pareto frontier in most configurations. Reasoning reaches the frontier only for open-ended output formats at 7B and above. A sequential curriculum with 25–50% reasoning data recovers most of the gain cheaply, and mixed training below 50% keeps IFT inference cost. The saturating fits are interpolation aids, not a claimed scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares IFT and reasoning-distilled post-training students using downstream accuracy and FLOPs, rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss or fitting the original pretraining scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream results vary with supervision format, training corpus, task format, and student size.

fits_no_version.finding: Inference FLOPs scale as a power of student size, with fitted exponents 0.58–0.94 for IFT and 0.68–0.85 for reasoning (Figure 14).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference cost of distilled students grows as a power law in model size, with exponents that depend on supervision format.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched training and inference FLOPs, larger IFT models lie on or near the Pareto frontier in most configurations. Reasoning reaches the frontier only on open-ended tasks at 7B and above.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under a fixed post-training compute budget, scaling model size beats lengthening supervision traces except for open-ended tasks at ≥7B.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The tested students reach at most 14B parameters. The accuracy curves are fitted to observed points, with no reported validation on withheld runs or substantially larger models. Judge error is summarized, but uncertainty for the scaling fits is not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional V6 rows were extracted for every individual Table 1 score or benchmark-level Figure 15–21 result; the included rows capture the paper's stated aggregate scale trends and reported fit. The remaining individual scores are in Table 1 and Figures 15–21.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss. Students are off-the-shelf pretrained Qwen2.5 and Gemma-3 bases.
No extrapolation from small runs is checked against larger runs.
No pretraining parameter/token compute-optimal split. Matched-FLOPs comparisons are between post-training formats.
Depth, width and other shape details are not varied at fixed parameter count.
No power-law loss fits in fine-tuning or other regimes.

Predictability from pretraining loss is not tested. Extrapolation of the saturating accuracy-vs-FLOPs fits beyond 14B is not validated. Scale is the size of the pretrained base, not a controlled pretraining sweep.
No comparison of fitted exponents or fitting choices for loss laws.

missing.what: Monotonic accuracy gains with size for reasoning-distilled students on the general-purpose corpus, e.g. Math-OE 22.4→43.7→55.4→66.3→74.7.
Monotonic accuracy gains with size for IFT and reasoning students on the math-centric corpus, e.g. Math-OE IFT 14.5→66.3, reasoning 9.2→81.3.
Replication with Gemma-3 students (1B, 4B, 12B) distilled from a Nemotron-Super-49B teacher: accuracy vs size and vs inference FLOPs.
Accuracy vs size and FLOPs on additional reasoning-intensive tasks (law, code, physics).

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3: this is a new setting (post-training distillation) whose size sweep bears on V6 only incidentally. Rows r2–r4 are format or corpus comparisons and are relinked to none. The single V6 'supports' verdict rests on r1. The record's limits_scope label is dropped: unvalidated fits are an untested part, and format crossovers do not bear on V6. Student scale is limited to 14B, and base models differ only by Qwen's own pretraining, so scale is not controlled.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run loss fit is evaluated against much larger training runs.
The study compares post-training formats at matched FLOPs; it does not find a loss-minimising parameter/token split for pretraining compute.
It does not hold parameter count fixed while varying depth, width, or other architecture details.
Although it studies instruction tuning and reasoning distillation, it does not test whether the same power-law form holds for loss in those regimes or in other modalities.

Tests downstream accuracy across student sizes and compute for IFT and reasoning distillation; does not test predictability from pretraining loss or validate extrapolations on held-out, substantially larger runs.
It does not compare fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations across setups or fitting choices.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 students (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, and 14B; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream accuracy across student sizes on the general-purpose corpus.
rows.measure: Average downstream accuracy as student size increases
rows.value: IFT improves steadily across all four task families, with consistent gains at each size step.
rows.note: Aggregate trend stated by the authors across the tested model sizes; individual scores are also reported in Table 1.
rows.check: Correct. Table 1 confirms monotonic gains, e.g. General-OE 24.9→37.0→52.2→56.4→66.1. The row covers only general-purpose IFT.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 students (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, and 14B; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream accuracy across student sizes and against IFT.
rows.measure: Downstream accuracy compared with IFT across scale-corpus configurations
rows.baseline: IFT models at the corresponding scale and corpus
rows.value: Reasoning outperforms IFT in 70% of scale-corpus configurations (28 out of 40 pairs), but not uniformly.
rows.note: This is the paper's aggregate comparison; it does not establish a single predictable scaling curve shared by the two supervision formats.
rows.check: This compares supervision formats at equal size (28/40 pairs), not how accuracy changes with scale. It does not measure V6.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 students (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, and 14B; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared general-domain downstream accuracy across sizes and training corpora.
rows.baseline: Reasoning models trained on the general-purpose corpus
rows.value: Math-centric reasoning lags well behind at smaller scales; the gap closes only partially by 14B.
rows.note: The size trend depends on training corpus; the text says standard IFT on the math-centric corpus does not show the same general-domain penalty.
rows.check: This is a corpus comparison: math-centric vs general-purpose reasoning on general tasks. Within that series accuracy still rises with size (General-OE 8.2→69.2), but the row records the gap, not the scale trend.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 students (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, and 14B; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared General-MC accuracy across student sizes and supervision formats.
rows.value: IFT leads at 0.5B; the formats are effectively tied at 1.5B; reasoning leads from 3B onward.
rows.note: The reported relative performance changes with student size.
rows.check: This is a format crossover (IFT vs reasoning) on General-MC, not a scaling measure. Both formats rise with size in Table 1.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 students (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, and 14B; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit accuracy against training and inference FLOPs for interpolation.
rows.measure: Downstream accuracy as a function of training FLOPs and inference FLOPs
rows.value: The observed data are fitted with a saturating growth function for interpolation; the paper reports Pareto-frontier comparisons between IFT and reasoning.
rows.note: The paper states the fitted function and fitting method, but does not report validation of predictions on withheld or much larger runs.
rows.check: The row reports only that a saturating curve was fitted (Appendix E, fitted by mean absolute error). No fit quality and no held-out prediction are reported, so predictability cannot be read. The fit form is the authors' choice, not evidence for or against a power law.

relationships.condition: Qwen2.5 students 0.5B–14B after IFT on the general-purpose corpus; downstream accuracy across four task families
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises at every size step in all four families (r1, Table 1). Table 1 also shows monotonic gains for reasoning and math-centric series, which are not yet rows (see missing).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased at every model-size step across all four task families, with monotonic gains also observed in reasoning and math-centric training series.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
